content.text:
Reviewed all 49 verbs in shard 28 (the *l*–*m* range) and wrote three findings to `verbdata/gloss-review/shards/gloss_028.out.json`.

**`losschlagen` — medium.** Shipped "knock loose", kaikki's first-listed sense, which is the technical literal one (loosening something by striking it). The sense a learner actually meets is *attack, strike* — sitting at index 2. Fix: `attack, strike`.

**`leichtfallen` — low.** Shipped "come, be easy". The comma here isn't separating synonyms; it's a fracture inside the phrase "come easy", so under the house convention the gloss advertises "come" as a meaning of *leichtfallen*. Fix: `come easily, be easy`.

**`losgehen` — low.** Shipped "leave", which collides with *verlassen* and invites the transitive reading a learner will then produce wrongly. Fix: `set off, get going`.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The `leichtfallen` case is a defect the importer couldn't have caught, because the comma came from kaikki intact — it only becomes wrong once it lands in a corpus whose house style reads commas as "these are synonyms." A punctuation mark changes meaning when the surrounding convention changes.
- `losschlagen` shows why `sense_index: 0` is a weak signal on its own: kaikki orders senses by compositional transparency (*los* + *schlagen* = strike loose) rather than frequency, so the most literal reading systematically sorts first and the idiomatic one — which is what German speakers actually say — sinks.
- The bulk of the shard is high-frequency simplexes (*lassen*, *laufen*, *machen*, *meinen*), and those all held up. The multi-sense commas there — "let, allow, leave", "delete, extinguish" — technically strain the synonym convention, but they match standard learner-dictionary practice and none would mislead, so they aren't findings.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`
